myth: India won independence through the work of only one or two leaders.

Millions of people took part, including farmers, workers, students and women who marched, went to jail or gave up their jobs. Leaders with very different ideas, from Gandhi and Nehru to Bose, Ambedkar and Patel, all shaped the result.

sec.t:
In 1885, a group of lawyers, teachers and journalists met in Bombay and formed the Indian National Congress. At first, they asked politely for more Indians in government and fairer taxes.

Some leaders wanted to push harder. [[@tilak|Bal Gangadhar Tilak]] is remembered for declaring that swaraj, self-rule, was his birthright. When the British divided Bengal in 1905, people answered with the Swadeshi movement, boycotting British goods. Rabindranath [[@tagore|Tagore]] wrote songs for the protests.

Not everyone followed Gandhi's methods. Young revolutionaries believed only force would drive out the British. Bhagat Singh and his comrades were hanged in 1931 and became heroes to millions.

B.R. Ambedkar fought for the rights of Dalits, people treated as "untouchable", and argued that freedom from Britain meant little without freedom from caste. Muslim leaders in the Muslim League, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, increasingly demanded a separate country. Women such as [[@sarojini-naidu|Sarojini Naidu]] and Aruna Asaf Ali led protests and went to jail.

sec.h: Quit India and the war years
sec.t:
During the Second World War, Britain brought India into the war without asking Indian leaders. On 8 August 1942, the Congress launched the [[@quit-india|Quit India Movement]]. Its leaders were arrested within hours, but protests spread across the country.

Meanwhile, Subhas Chandra Bose led the [[@indian-national-army|Indian National Army]], fighting alongside Japan against the British. When INA officers were put on trial in Delhi in 1945, there were huge public protests. In 1946, sailors of the Royal Indian Navy mutinied in Bombay.

By 1946, Britain was exhausted by war and could no longer hold India. Talks between the Congress, the Muslim League and the British failed to agree on a united country.

On 15 August 1947, India became independent, and Pakistan was created a day earlier. [[partition|Partition]] forced around 1.5 crore people to flee their homes, and hundreds of thousands were killed in riots. On 26 January 1950, India adopted its [[@constitution|Constitution]] and became a [[republic|republic]], exactly twenty years after the promise of complete freedom.

text: India's first postage stamp was the Scinde Dawk, issued on 1 July 1852 in the province of Sindh, now in Pakistan. It was a small round stamp, worth half an anna, with the emblem of the East India Company pressed into it. "Dawk" was the British spelling of the Hindi word *dak*, meaning post.

It was the first postage stamp in Asia. Only about 12 years earlier, in 1840, Britain had issued the world's first, the Penny Black. Two years after the Scinde Dawk, in 1854, stamps were issued for the whole of British India.

sec.t:
Before stamps, letters in India were usually paid for by the person receiving them. The price depended on distance and weight, and post office clerks had to work it out by hand. It was slow, confusing and easy to cheat.

Sir Bartle Frere, the British official in charge of Sindh, wanted something simpler. He had seen how Britain's new stamps worked. If senders paid in advance with a small sticker, the post could move faster and more reliably. So in 1852 he brought out the Scinde Dawk.

Frere also reformed the old system of runners and camel riders that carried mail across the deserts of Sindh. He set up a regular postal service, with fixed routes and timetables, and the new stamp was part of making it work.

On 1 October 1854, the [[@post-office|post office]] of British India issued its first stamps for the whole country. They showed Queen Victoria and came in values of half an anna, one anna, two annas and four annas. A letter could now travel anywhere in British India for one flat price, depending only on weight.

The four anna stamp was printed in two colours, red and blue, in two separate runs. On a few sheets, the queen's head was printed upside down. These "inverted head" stamps are now worth a fortune to collectors, because so few were made.

After independence, India needed new stamps. On 21 November 1947, the first stamp of independent India came out. It showed the new national flag, with the words "Jai Hind". It cost three and a half annas.

Later Indian stamps have shown Mahatma Gandhi, tigers, satellites, cricketers, temples, festivals and famous scientists. Some celebrated India's space missions, others its [[@national-symbols|national symbols]]. India Post has issued thousands of different designs since 1947. In 1948, India issued four stamps in memory of Gandhi, a year after independence. Collectors prize them today, especially a rare version printed only for use by the Governor-General's office.

Collecting stamps is called philately. Stamp collectors study paper, ink, perforations (the little holes between stamps) and postmarks. A single tiny error can make a stamp very valuable.

Even in the age of email, stamps are still printed and collected. Special postmarks, like the boat design used at the [[@oddity-floating-post-office|floating post office]] on Dal Lake, turn an ordinary envelope into something people want to keep.

text: When the USA raced the Soviet Union in the [[@space-race|space race]], it needed huge amounts of maths. How fast must a rocket go? At what angle should a capsule come back so it neither bounces off the air nor burns up? Much of this was worked out by hand, with pencils, slide rules and desk calculators.

Many of the people doing those sums were women. Some of the best were Black women at [[@nasa-centres|NASA's Langley centre]] in Virginia, who worked in a separate unit because of [[@civil-rights|segregation laws]]. [[@usa-nasa-hidden-figures|Katherine Johnson]], Dorothy Vaughan and Mary Jackson were three of them. Their story became widely known through the 2016 book and film *Hidden Figures*.

sec.t:
Before electronic machines took over, "computer" was a job title. From 1935, the aircraft research agency NACA, which later became NASA, hired women to check data from wind tunnels and test flights. The work was careful and repetitive, and it needed real skill.

During the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], more workers were needed, and Langley began hiring Black women with maths degrees. Virginia's laws kept them apart. They worked in the "West Area" unit, ate at a separate table, and used separate bathrooms. Their work, though, went into the same aircraft and rockets as everyone else's.

Katherine Johnson loved numbers from childhood and finished high school at 14. At Langley she worked on the maths of flight paths, called trajectories. She calculated the path for Alan Shepard, the first American in space, in 1961.

The next year, John Glenn prepared to become the first American to [[orbit|orbit]] the Earth. NASA's electronic computers had worked out his route, but Glenn wanted it checked. According to NASA's history, he asked for Johnson by name. She checked the numbers by hand, and they agreed. Later she helped with calculations for the [[@apollo-moon|Apollo]] [[@moon-landing-sites|Moon landings]]. In 2015 she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

Mary Jackson began as a computer in the West Area. An engineer noticed her talent and encouraged her to train as an engineer herself. The classes she needed were held at an all-white school, so she had to get special permission from the city to attend. In 1958 she became NASA's first Black woman engineer. Later she worked to help other women and minorities get hired and promoted.

At the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Margaret Hamilton led the team that wrote software for the Apollo guidance computer. During the first Moon landing in 1969, alarms flashed as the computer was flooded with tasks. Her team's software was designed to drop less important jobs and keep going, and the landing went ahead.

India has its own story. Women scientists and engineers helped lead ISRO's Mars Orbiter Mission in 2014 and the [[@chandrayaan|Chandrayaan]] missions to the Moon, doing the same kind of careful calculation, now with far faster machines.

text: The Kailasa temple at Ellora, near Aurangabad in Maharashtra, was made in the 8th century under the Rashtrakutas, a [[dynasty|dynasty]] that ruled much of the Deccan from about 753 to 982 CE. It is usually credited to King Krishna I, who ruled from about 756 to 774.

The temple is dedicated to Shiva and named after Mount Kailash, his home in the Himalaya. It was cut from a single [[basalt|basalt]] hillside. Workers carved deep trenches on three sides of a huge block of rock, then shaped that block into a temple, complete with a tall shrine, halls, pillars, bridges and life-size elephants. Experts often estimate that around 200,000 tonnes of rock were removed.

It was carved out of one solid mass of rock. The workers cut trenches around a block of hillside, then hollowed and shaped it into halls, pillars, bridges and statues.

sec.t:
The Rashtrakutas started as officials under the [[@chalukyas|Chalukyas]] of Badami. Around 753, a chief named Dantidurga rebelled, defeated his overlords and set up his own kingdom. His uncle, Krishna I, took over soon after and expanded it.

At their height, the Rashtrakutas ruled from Gujarat to Tamil Nadu. Their later capital was Manyakheta, today's Malkhed in Karnataka. They fought constantly with two rivals, the Pratiharas of the north and the Palas of Bengal, over the rich city of Kannauj on the Ganga. None of the three ever won for good.

Most buildings go up from the ground. Kailasa went down. Workers started at the top of the hill and cut their way towards the floor, so they finished the tower before the base.

The main shrine rises about 30 metres, as tall as a ten-storey building. Inside the rock, sculptors left pillars to hold up halls and carved stone bridges between the parts of the temple. Around the courtyard, the walls are covered with scenes from the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] and the [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]]. A famous panel shows the demon king Ravana shaking Mount Kailash while Shiva calmly holds it steady with one toe.

There was no room for big mistakes. Every pillar and doorway had to be planned before the first chisel touched the rock.

{{story:deccan}}

Ellora's rock is basalt, a dark stone formed from [[lava|lava]]. About 66 million years ago, enormous volcanic eruptions poured layer after layer of lava over western India, creating the [[@deccan|Deccan]] Traps. The cliffs at Ellora and Ajanta are made of these layers.

Basalt is hard but even, which made it good for detailed carving. Traces of plaster and paint show that the temple was once painted, possibly white, to look like a snow-covered Himalayan peak.

An Arab merchant named Sulaiman, who wrote in 851, listed the Rashtrakuta king as one of the four great kings of the world, alongside the rulers of Baghdad, China and Constantinople.

That king was probably Amoghavarsha I, who ruled for over 60 years. He was a patron of writers in Sanskrit and [[@kannada-telugu|Kannada]]. The *Kavirajamarga*, one of the oldest surviving works on Kannada poetry, is linked to his court. He was also deeply interested in Jainism, and Jain caves at Ellora were carved in this period.

Ellora has 34 main caves along a two-kilometre cliff. The Buddhist caves are the oldest, followed by Hindu caves, including Kailasa, and then Jain caves. Monks, priests and pilgrims of different faiths worked and worshipped side by side for centuries.

The Rashtrakutas lost power in 973, when the Western Chalukyas overthrew them. The last of the family to claim the throne died in 982. Their temple remained. A thousand years later, visitors still stand in its courtyard and look up at a building made by taking rock away.

text: Ruby Bridges is an American woman who, as a six-year-old in 1960, became the first Black child to attend William Frantz Elementary School in New Orleans, Louisiana. Until then, it had been a school for white children only.

Her first day, on 14 November 1960, became one of the most famous moments of the American [[@civil-rights|civil rights]] movement. Crowds of adults shouted at her. Four US marshals, sent by the [[federal|federal]] government, walked her up the steps. She went back every day, for the whole year.
Today Ruby Bridges travels and speaks to schoolchildren about fairness and getting along.

st.reveal: Almost all the white families kept their children home or moved them to other schools. For most of the year Ruby sat in a classroom with only her teacher, Barbara Henry.

d.try: Ruby Bridges was six. Ask a grown-up in your family what they remember about their first day at a new school. Then write or draw your own first-day memory, and compare how each of you felt.
myth: After the US Supreme Court banned school segregation in 1954, schools were mixed straight away.
Many states and school boards resisted for years. Six years later, Ruby Bridges still needed federal marshals to get through the door, and some schools stayed segregated well into the 1970s.
facts: The Problem We All Live With, Norman Rockwell, 1964

sec.t:
In the American South, Black and white children went to separate schools, by law. Schools for Black children usually got less money, older books and fewer teachers. In 1954, the US Supreme Court ruled in a case called Brown v. Board of Education that this was against the Constitution.

But many places dragged their feet. New Orleans did not begin mixing its schools until 1960, and only after a judge ordered it. Black children who wanted to transfer had to pass a hard test. Ruby passed. She was one of only six chosen, and two of the six later decided not to go.

The other three girls started at a different school that same morning. Ruby went to William Frantz alone.

{{story:courage}}

When Ruby arrived, almost all the white parents pulled their children out. Many teachers refused to teach her. One agreed: Barbara Henry, a young teacher who had just moved from Boston.

For most of the year, Mrs Henry and Ruby sat in a classroom together, just the two of them. They read, did sums and played games. Ruby has said she did not understand at first why the school was so empty. She was not even allowed to go out to play at break, for her safety.

Every morning, protesters waited outside. Ruby later said she thought the noise was like Mardi Gras, the big carnival that fills [[@new-orleans|New Orleans]] with parades.

sec.h: A family that paid a price
sec.t:
Standing up cost Ruby's family dearly. Her father lost his job at a petrol station. Her grandparents, who farmed in Mississippi, were forced off the land they had worked on. A local shop told her family not to come back.

But many people helped too. Neighbours, both Black and white, babysat, watched the house and walked behind the marshals' car. A child doctor named Robert Coles met Ruby every week to talk about how she was feeling. He was struck by one thing she told him: she prayed every day for the people shouting at her.

sec.h: The painting in the White House
sec.t:
In 1964, the American artist Norman Rockwell painted a picture of Ruby's walk to school. It shows a small girl in a white dress and shoes, with a ruler and pencils, between four tall marshals whose faces are cut off by the frame. Behind her is a wall with a thrown tomato and an ugly slur scrawled on it.

The painting, called The Problem We All Live With, is now one of the most [[@famous-paintings|famous paintings]] in American history. In 2011, it hung outside the Oval Office in the White House, and Ruby, then in her fifties, stood beside it.

By the second year, more children came back to the school, both Black and white. Ruby finished elementary school there, later worked as a travel agent, and raised four sons. In 1999 she started the Ruby Bridges Foundation to promote respect between children of all backgrounds.

Her story sits alongside other ordinary people who refused to back down. Five years earlier, [[@rosa-parks|Rosa Parks]] had refused to give up her seat on a bus in Montgomery, Alabama.

text: In October 1871, the Great Chicago Fire destroyed the centre of the city. It burned for about two days, killed around 300 people and left about 100,000 homeless. Most buildings had been made of wood, and a long dry summer and strong winds helped the flames spread.

Chicago rebuilt fast, and land in the centre became very expensive. To fit more offices on each plot, architects built upwards. In 1885, the Home Insurance Building used a frame of iron and steel to hold up its floors, instead of thick stone walls. That idea made tall buildings possible, and many people call it the first skyscraper.

st.prompt: In 1900, Chicago's engineers did something strange to the Chicago River. What?

options.t: They made it flow backwards
They covered it with a roof
They dyed it green for good

st.reveal: Sewage was flowing into Lake Michigan, where the city got its drinking water. Engineers dug a canal so the river would flow away from the lake, towards the Mississippi. It still flows that way today.

d.try: Build a paper skyscraper. Using only paper and tape, build the tallest tower you can that stands on its own. Then try again, rolling paper into tubes to make a frame first. Which tower is taller and stronger? Chicago's builders learned the same lesson with steel.
myth: The Great Chicago Fire started when Mrs O'Leary's cow kicked over a lantern.

A newspaper reporter later admitted he made up the cow story. The fire did begin near the O'Learys' barn, but its exact cause is unknown. In 1997 the Chicago City Council officially cleared Catherine O'Leary and her cow.

sec.t:
Before the fire, Chicago was a young city that had grown very quickly. It sat where railways from the east met the farmland of the west, and where [[@great-lakes|Lake Michigan]] connected to rivers leading to the Mississippi. Grain, timber and cattle all passed through.

After the fire, the city passed rules against wooden buildings in the centre. Architects and engineers rushed in from across the country. They had a blank space, rich clients and new materials such as steel. The [[@fire-burns|fire]] had cleared the way for a new kind of city.

In 1973, the Sears Tower, now called the Willis Tower, was finished. At about 442 m, it was the tallest building in the world for 25 years. It is made of nine square tubes bundled together, a design by the engineer Fazlur Rahman Khan, who was born in what is now [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]]. His tube designs made very tall [[@skyscrapers|skyscrapers]] cheaper to build, and many later towers used them.

On a glass ledge called the Skydeck, you can stand on the 103rd floor and look straight down through the floor.

In the 1800s, Chicago dumped its sewage into the Chicago River, which flowed into Lake Michigan, where the city got its drinking water. People got sick from water-borne diseases. So in 1900, engineers opened a canal that reversed the river, sending it away from the lake. Every year on St Patrick's Day, the river is dyed bright green for a few hours.

In 1893, Chicago hosted the World's Columbian Exposition, a giant fair. It showed off the world's first Ferris wheel, about 80 m tall. At the Parliament of the World's Religions, held alongside it, Swami [[@swami-vivekananda|Vivekananda]] gave a [[@speeches-famous|famous speech]] that began "Sisters and Brothers of America". It introduced many Americans to Hindu ideas and Indian thought about [[@religions-world|world religions]].

Chicago is also known for [[@blues|blues]] and jazz, for its "deep-dish" [[@pizza|pizza]], baked in a high-sided pan, and for icy winds blowing off the lake in winter.

text: The biggest island in the world is [[@world-greenland|Greenland]], in the far North Atlantic. It covers about 2.2 million square kilometres, roughly two-thirds the size of India. Most of it is covered by a thick sheet of ice.

You might wonder about Australia, which is bigger still. Geographers usually count Australia as a continent rather than an island, so Greenland takes the top spot. After Greenland come New Guinea, Borneo and [[@madagascar|Madagascar]]. Together, the world's islands hold about one in ten of all the people on Earth.

st.prompt: On many world maps, Greenland and Africa look about the same size. How big is Africa really, compared with Greenland?

options.t: About 14 times bigger
About the same size
About twice as big

st.reveal: Africa covers about 30 million square kilometres and Greenland about 2.2 million. Common maps stretch lands near the poles, so Greenland looks far bigger than it is.

d.try: Peel an orange in as few pieces as you can, then try to flatten the peel on a table. It tears and stretches, especially near the top and bottom. Mapmakers face the same problem when they flatten the round Earth onto paper.
myth: Greenland is about as big as Africa.
Greenland only looks huge because many maps stretch places near the poles. Africa is about 14 times bigger. India, at about 3.3 million square kilometres, is also bigger than Greenland.

sec.t:
Greenland is an island of rock, but you would hardly know it. About 80% is buried under an ice sheet up to about 3 km thick. [[@what-if-ice-melted|If all that ice melted]], the world's seas would rise by about 7 m.

Only about 56,000 people live there, mostly Inuit, in towns along the coast. Greenland is a self-governing [[territory|territory]] within the Kingdom of Denmark. Its capital, Nuuk, is home to about a third of the people. There are no roads linking the towns, so people travel by boat, plane, helicopter, snowmobile or dog sled.

Islands form in a few main ways. Some were once part of a continent and were cut off by [[@sea-level-rise|rising seas]] or drifting [[plate|plates]]. [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]], Great Britain and Madagascar are like this.

Others are built by volcanoes rising from the sea floor, such as Hawaii and [[@iceland|Iceland]], as you can read in [[@hawaii-islands|Hawaii's islands]]. A third kind is made by living things. Tiny [[@coral-bleaching|coral animals]] build reefs that, over thousands of years, become low islands of sand, like India's [[@lakshadweep|Lakshadweep]] and the [[@maldives|Maldives]]. Rivers make islands too. [[@majuli|Majuli]], in the Brahmaputra in Assam, is one of the biggest river islands in the world.

New Guinea, the second-largest island, is split between two countries: Papua New Guinea in the east and Indonesia in the west. It has some of the world's most varied languages, more than 800 on one island, and birds of paradise with spectacular feathers.

Borneo, the third, is shared by three countries: Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei. Its rainforests are home to orangutans, one of the great apes. Borneo also has the world's biggest flower, the rafflesia, which can grow almost a metre wide and smells like rotting meat to attract flies. Madagascar, the fourth-largest island, broke away from India about 88 million years ago.

Islands often have animals and plants found nowhere else. Cut off from the mainland, living things change over many generations to suit their new homes. Madagascar has lemurs. The [[@galapagos|Galápagos]] has giant tortoises. Mauritius had the [[@dodo|dodo]], a flightless bird that vanished after people arrived in the 1600s.

India has many islands of its own. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands, in the Bay of Bengal, number over 800. They are home to ancient forests, [[@india-wonder-andaman-reefs|coral reefs]] and some of the most isolated peoples on Earth.

text: Vietnam is a long, narrow country on the eastern edge of mainland Southeast Asia. It curves like a letter S for about 1,650 kilometres, from the mountains on the Chinese border down to the flat, watery Mekong Delta. At its narrowest point it is only about 50 kilometres wide.

About 10 crore people live there. The capital, Hanoi, is in the north, and the biggest city, Ho Chi Minh City, is in the south. Vietnam is known for green rice paddies, limestone islands rising from the sea, noodle soup for breakfast, strong coffee and streets full of motorbikes. To many older Americans, Vietnam also means a long and painful war that ended in 1975.

A tree
A moving boat on the open sea

st.reveal: In water puppetry, puppeteers stand waist-deep in water behind a bamboo screen. They move wooden puppets on long poles hidden under the surface, so the puppets seem to swim, fish and dance on the water by themselves.

myth: Vietnamese is written with Chinese characters.
For centuries Vietnamese scholars did write in Chinese characters. Today Vietnamese uses the Latin alphabet, with extra marks above and below letters to show its six tones.

about 1,650 km from north to south

sec.h: Two rice baskets on a pole
sec.t:
People often describe Vietnam as two rice baskets hanging from a carrying pole. The baskets are the two great river deltas: the Red River Delta in the north and the Mekong Delta in the south. Both are flat and [[fertile|fertile]], crisscrossed by canals, and covered in [[@rice|rice]] paddies.

The pole is the narrow middle, squeezed between mountains and the sea. Vietnam grows so much rice that it is one of the world's biggest exporters. In the Mekong Delta, families sell fruit and vegetables from boats at floating markets, and children may go to school by canoe.

sec.h: Puppets on water and an alphabet from abroad
sec.t:
Water puppetry began in the Red River Delta about a thousand years ago, when farmers performed in flooded rice paddies after the harvest. Today it is staged in theatres with a pool of water as the stage. The [[@puppetry|puppeteers]] hide behind a bamboo screen and work the puppets with long poles under the water.

For centuries, Vietnamese was written in [[@chinese-characters|Chinese characters]]. In the 1600s, European missionaries worked with Vietnamese helpers to write the language in Latin letters, with accent marks to show its six tones. In the early 1900s this script, called chữ Quốc ngữ, became the main way of writing Vietnamese, part of a long story in the [[@alphabet-history|history of the alphabet]].

In the 20th century Vietnam fought France for independence, then was split into north and south. The Vietnam War, between the communist north and the US-backed south, became one of the most violent conflicts of the [[@cold-war|Cold War]]. It cost millions of lives and ended in 1975 when the country was reunited under the north.

Since the 1980s, Vietnam has opened up to world trade and grown fast. It is now the second-biggest coffee producer in the world, after Brazil. Vietnamese iced coffee is made with sweetened condensed milk, strong and sweet enough to keep you awake through a hot afternoon.

text: *Little Women* is a novel by the American writer Louisa May Alcott, published in two parts in 1868 and 1869. It follows four sisters, Meg, Jo, Beth and Amy March, as they grow up in a small Massachusetts town while their father is away serving in the [[@us-civil-war|American Civil War]].

It is still read because the sisters feel real. They quarrel, make mistakes, worry about money, fall in love and chase dreams. Jo, who wants to be a writer and hates being told how girls should behave, has been a hero to readers for more than 150 years. The book has never gone out of print and has been made into films, plays, TV series and an opera.

st.prompt: Jo March, the hero of Little Women, was based on a real person. Who?

options.t: Louisa May Alcott herself
The first female US president

st.reveal: Like Jo, Alcott was a tomboy who loved writing and plays, sold stories to help her family and refused to fit in. The other sisters were also based on Alcott's own sisters, Anna, Lizzie and May.

myth: Louisa May Alcott always dreamed of writing a story for girls.
She wrote it because her publisher asked. In her journal she said she found it dull work and had never known many girls except her sisters. She drew on her own family to make it real.
facts: a town in Massachusetts, USA, during the Civil War
Meg, Jo, Beth and Amy March

sec.t:
Alcott was not a rich, comfortable author. Her family was poor, and she had been writing to support them since she was young, including sensational thrillers under a false name.

In 1867, a publisher named Thomas Niles asked her to write a book for girls. She wasn't keen. In her journal she wrote that she was plodding on, didn't enjoy it and had never known many girls except her sisters. So she wrote about them.

She wrote at Orchard House, the family home in Concord, Massachusetts, near [[@boston|Boston]]. Part one was a success, and readers demanded more. She wrote part two in a few months.

{{story:us-civil-war}}

Each March sister wants something different. Meg, the eldest, longs for pretty things and a family of her own. Jo wants to write and to be free. Beth, shy and gentle, loves music and her home. Amy, the youngest, wants to be an artist and to be admired.

The book doesn't say one dream is right. It lets each sister grow in her own way. Many readers argue for years about which sister they are most like. The sisters also make their own fun. They stage dramatic home-made plays, with Jo happily playing the villains, a small slice of [[@theatre|theatre]] in a cold parlour. They even run a family newspaper.

The family also struggles. Their father is away at war, and money is short. When Beth falls seriously ill, the story becomes heartbreaking. Alcott's own sister Lizzie had died young, and the sadness in those chapters is real.

Alcott's family believed strongly in fairness. They were opponents of [[@slavery-freedom|slavery]], and their homes sheltered at least one person escaping slavery. During the Civil War, Louisa worked as a nurse in a Union army hospital in Washington, until she caught typhoid fever and was sent home. Her letters became a book, *Hospital Sketches*.

She also supported women's right to vote. In 1879, when women in Massachusetts were allowed to vote in elections for school boards, she was the first woman to register in Concord. Women across the USA would not get the full [[@womens-vote|vote]] until 1920, more than 30 years after she died.

Readers keep finding new things in *Little Women*. Some love it for its warmth and family life. Others read it for Jo's ambition and her refusal to be squeezed into a small life.

In 2019, the director Greta Gerwig made a film that made Alcott's own struggles part of the story. It brought a new wave of readers. Like Jo writing plays in the attic, Alcott took the people around her and turned them into a story that has outlived them all.

text: The Nobel Prize in Literature is one of the world's best-known awards for writers. It has been given almost every year since 1901, to a novelist, poet, playwright or essayist whose work the judges consider outstanding.

It was set up by the will of Alfred Nobel, a Swedish chemist who [[@accident-dynamite|invented dynamite]] and became very rich. When he died in 1896, he left most of his fortune to fund prizes in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace. The literature prize is chosen by the Swedish Academy in Stockholm. The winner receives a gold medal, a diploma and a large sum of money, about 11 million Swedish kronor in recent years.

st.prompt: The Nobel Prize in Literature is usually given for what?

options.t: A writer's whole body of work
The best-selling book of the year
The best new book published that year

st.reveal: Unlike most book prizes, the Nobel honours a writer, not a single book. The citation often mentions what is special about their writing over many years. Tagore's 1913 citation praised his "beautiful verse" in general, though Gitanjali was the book the judges had read.

n.certNote: The rules and history of the prize are clear. Which writers deserved it, and which were wrongly left out, is a matter of endless argument, as with any prize decided by a small group of judges.

sec.t:
Each year, the Swedish Academy invites nominations from qualified people: literature professors, members of similar academies, past winners and heads of writers' organisations. Writers can't nominate themselves. There are usually a few hundred nominations.

A small committee narrows these down to a shortlist of about five. Over the summer, Academy members read the shortlisted writers' works, often in [[@translation|translation]]. In October they vote, and the winner is announced at a press conference in Stockholm. The names of nominees are kept secret for 50 years.

The prize is handed over on 10 December, the anniversary of Nobel's death, at a ceremony in Stockholm. Each winner also gives a Nobel lecture, and many of these speeches are famous in their own right.

The Academy has often surprised people. In 1953, it gave the prize to Winston Churchill, Britain's wartime prime minister, for his history writing and speeches. In 2016 it went to Bob Dylan, the American singer, "for having created new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition". Some people cheered. Others said songs aren't literature.

Two writers turned the prize down. Jean-Paul Sartre declined it in 1964, saying a writer shouldn't become an institution. Boris Pasternak, author of Doctor Zhivago, was forced by the Soviet government to refuse it in 1958.

In 2018, no prize was announced at first, after a scandal inside the Academy. The next year two winners were named, one for 2018 and one for 2019.

Critics point out that most winners have been men from Europe and North America. Great writers like Leo Tolstoy, Anton Chekhov and Virginia Woolf never won. Writers in less widely translated languages have a harder time getting noticed.

That has slowly been changing. Toni Morrison became the first Black woman to win in 1993, and the South Korean writer Han Kang became the first Asian woman to win in 2024. Like the [[@nobel-peace|Nobel Peace Prize]] and the science prizes that [[@marie-curie|Marie Curie]] won twice, the literature prize gets more attention than almost any other award in its field. For many writers, it changes everything overnight.

text: Jalebi is a swirl of fermented batter, fried until crisp and dunked in sugar syrup. It feels completely Indian, from Diwali boxes to winter mornings with hot milk. But its story most likely starts in West Asia.

An Arabic cookbook from the 900s describes zalabiya, latticed fritters soaked in honey and rosewater. Food historians think this sweet travelled to India with traders, cooks and rulers from Persia and Central Asia, probably during [[medieval|medieval]] times. The name jalebi probably comes from the Arabic zulabiya or the Persian zolbiya. By about 1450, an Indian Jain text was already mentioning it. Since then, India has invented dozens of versions.

st.prompt: Jalebi batter is often left to sit for hours before frying. Why?

options.t: So it ferments and gets slightly sour and bubbly
So the flour turns orange by itself
So it becomes too thick to pour

st.reveal: Traditional jalebi batter is left to ferment, often overnight. Wild yeasts and bacteria make tiny bubbles and a gentle sour taste. That makes the jalebi crisp and light, and balances the sweet syrup.

myth: Jalebi was invented in India and never left.
Similar fried, syrup-soaked swirls are eaten from Morocco to Iran to Nepal, and the oldest written recipes come from West Asia. India made jalebi its own, with countless local versions.

sec.t:
Nobody knows the exact day jalebi arrived. Persian-speaking traders and rulers had strong links with India for centuries, and cooks moved with them. Historians think the sweet came along one of these routes.

Historians have found a Jain work from about 1450 that mentions jalebi being served at a feast. A Sanskrit cookery text written before 1600 gives a recipe much like today's, using wheat flour batter and sugar syrup.

The batter is made from maida (refined wheat flour), sometimes with gram flour and curd. It is left to [[@fermentation|ferment]], often overnight. [[yeast|Yeasts]] and [[bacteria|bacteria]] eat a little of the starch and release gas, so the batter fills with tiny bubbles.

A cook squeezes it through a cloth or a bottle with a small hole into hot oil, drawing loops by hand. The bubbles make it crisp and full of tiny holes. While it is still hot, it goes into warm [[@sugar|sugar]] syrup, which soaks into all those holes. A good jalebi crackles when you bite it, then floods your mouth with syrup. Many sweet shops add a pinch of saffron or food colour for the bright orange shade, while homemade jalebi is often pale gold.

India has turned one sweet into many. In Bengal it is jilapi. Madhya Pradesh is famous for mawa jalebi, made with milk solids, often credited to a sweet maker in Jabalpur in 1889. Imarti, also called jangiri, is made from urad dal and shaped like a flower. Odisha makes chhena jalebi from fresh cheese.

People eat it differently too. In Indore, crowds gather for jalebi and poha at breakfast. In parts of north India, hot jalebi is dipped into rabri or milk in winter. Gujarat has a famous pairing: hot jalebi with fafda, a crunchy, salty strip made from gram flour. On the morning of Dussehra, sweet shops in Ahmedabad and Surat have long queues as families buy both to share.

Fried swirls soaked in syrup are found from North Africa to Nepal. In Nepal, a version is called jeri. Some people even link the funnel cake sold at American fairs to this family of sweets, though that link is not certain.

Jalebi is one sweet among many that came to India and were transformed. And the strangest part? Gulab jamun has a similar story, a Persian-inspired treat that India turned into its own, as you'll find in the tale of [[@food-gulab-jamun|gulab jamun]].
